Bayesian estimation
In the previous lesson, we consider parameter \(\theta\) as being fixed but unknown value and we were looking for point estimators for this \(\theta\). Now suppose we know some information about parameter before the experiment, more precisely we know its distribution.
Let's consider the following situation. We have two coins: one is fair (F) and another is biased (B), which shows Heads with probability \(0.2\). We pick one at random and start tossing. Since we have two coins, and they are equally likely to be chosen, the prior probability distribution is
\[\mathsf P(F)=0.5\]\[\mathsf P(B)=0.5\]
Suppose after 10 tosses, we got 6 Heads, denote this event by \(A\). Now let's find what is the probability that we choose fair coin given that we got \(6\) Heads in \(10\) tosses \[\mathsf P(F\mid A)=\frac{\mathsf P (A\mid F)\mathsf P(F)}{\mathsf P(A)}= \frac{(C_{10}^6\cdot 0.5^{6}0.5^{4})\cdot 0.5}{(C_{10}^6\cdot 0.5^{6}0.5^{4})\cdot 0.5+(C_{10}^6\cdot 0.2^{6}0.8^{4})\cdot 0.5} \propto \mathsf P(A\mid F)\mathsf P(F) = 0.5^{6}0.5^{4}\cdot 0.5\] where sign \(\propto\) means that \(\mathsf P(F\mid A)\) is proportional to the function \(\mathsf P (A\mid F)\mathsf P(F)\) (up to a constant factor \(\frac{1}{\mathsf P(A)}\)).
Analogously, we can find the probability that we choose the biased coin.\[\mathsf P(B\mid A)=\frac{\mathsf P(A\mid B)\mathsf P(B)}{\mathsf P(A)}= \propto \mathsf P(A\mid B)\mathsf P(B) = 0.2^{6}0.8^{4}\cdot 0.5\]
Thus \(\mathsf P(B\mid A)< \mathsf P(F\mid A)\) and odds have become \(\mathsf P(B\mid A): \mathsf P(F\mid A)\) in favour for a fair coin.
Bayesian approach:
A parameter \(\theta\) in the parametric distribution family \(f(\cdot \mid \theta)\) is unknown and drawn from prior distribution \(\Theta \sim \pi(\theta)\)
After seeing the data \(\mathbf x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)\), update information on \(\Theta\): consider its posterior distribution \(\pi (\theta \mid \mathbf x)\) (\(\equiv\) conditioned on \(\mathbf x\) ) \[ \pi(\theta \mid \mathbf x) \propto \pi(\theta) \cdot f_{\mathbf X}( \mathbf x \mid \theta) \]
Estimates of \(\theta\) must be based on the posterior distribution, not the prior one.
In the previous example we have sample \(\mathbf x = (x_1,\dots,x_{10})\) of size 10 from Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(p\).  The prior probability distributionof \(p\) is \[\pi(p)= \begin{cases} 0.5, & p=0.5\\ 0.5, & p=0.2\\ \end{cases}\] The posterior probability distributionof \(p\) is \[\pi(p\mid \mathbf x)= \begin{cases} \frac{0.5^{6}0.5^{4}}{0.5^{6}0.5^{4}+ 0.2^{6}0.8^{4}} , & p=0.5\\ \frac{0.2^{6}0.8^{4}}{0.5^{6}0.5^{4}+ 0.2^{6}0.8^{4}}, & p=0.2\\ \end{cases}\]
Note that in the Bayesian approach \(\theta\) is a random variable; we know its prior and posterior distribution. But what if we want to know an estimate for \(\theta\). For instance, in the case with fair and biased coins, we want to decide what coin is fair. Obviously using the posterior distribution we can conclude that tossed coin is fair. Here we used the maximum likelihood approach, we chose \(p\) which is the most probable.
As estimators for \(\theta\) we can use mean, median, or mode. Which one is the best?
Loss function
Assume that \(L(\hat{\theta},\theta)\) describes a loss function for suggesting an estimate \(\hat{\theta}\) for a true value \(\theta\).
Typical examples are
quadratic loss \(L(\hat{\theta},\theta) = (\hat{\theta} - \theta)^2\) (used by default )
absolute loss \(L(\hat{\theta},\theta) = |\hat{\theta}-\theta|\)
discrete loss \(L(\hat{\theta},\theta)\) = \(\begin{cases} 0, \qquad & \hat{\theta} = \theta;\\ 1, \qquad &\hat{\theta}\ne \theta \end{cases} \)
Definition. Bayesian estimate
Assume that \(\Theta\) has a prior distribution \(\pi\) and that data \(\mathbf x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)\) were sampled from distribution \(f(x\mid \theta)\). Then a Bayesian estimate \(\hat{\theta}(\mathbf x)\) of \(\theta\) for observation \(\mathbf x\) and loss function \(L(\hat{\theta},\theta)\) is the value \(\hat{\theta}\) that minimizes the mean posterior loss \[ \mathsf E_{\Theta\mid \mathbf x }(L(\hat{\theta},\theta)) \]
Let's consider our example with coins and find a Bayesian estimate under discrete loss. \[ \mathsf E_{P \mid \mathbf x }(L(\hat{p},p)) =\] since our posterior distributions is disctere \[ =\sum_{p} L(\hat{p},p)) \pi(p\mid \mathbf x) \] under discrete loss \[ =\sum_{ p\ne \hat{p}} \pi(p\mid \mathbf x). \] Now let's find \(\hat{p}\) which minimize this loss. Note that for \(\hat{p}=0.2\) the sum above  is equal  to \( \pi(0.5\mid \mathbf x)\), for \(\hat{p}=0.5\) the sum above  is equal \( \pi(0.2\mid \mathbf x)\),  and for any other  \(\hat{p}\)  this sum is equal to \( \pi(0.2\mid \mathbf x)+ \pi(0.5\mid \mathbf x)=1\). Hence \(\hat{p}=0.5\) minimizes  mean posterior loss.
Lemma
The Bayesian estimate is
posterior mean for quadratic loss;
posterior median for absolute loss;
posterior MLE for discrete loss
Note that \[ \mathsf{E}_{\Theta\mid \mathbf x } (\widehat\Theta-\theta)^2 = (\mathsf{E}_{\Theta\mid \mathbf x }  \theta - \widehat{\Theta}))^2 + \mathsf{Var}_{\Theta\mid \mathbf x }  \theta \] Thus Bayesian estimate under quadratic loss will be \[\widehat{\Theta} =\mathsf{E}_{\Theta\mid \mathbf x }  \theta \]

Problem 1.1 solution
Problem 1.1
The lifetimes (in hours) of computer chips produced by a certain semiconductor firm are exponentially distributed with parameter \(\lambda\). Suppose that the prior distribution on \(\lambda\) is the Gamma distribution with parameters \((3,1)\). If the average life of the first \(20\) chips tested is \(4.6\) hours, find posterior density \(\pi(\lambda \mid \mathbf x)\) and identify it.
Solution.
We have sample \(X_1,\dots, X_{20}\) of size \(20\) from population with exponential distribution with  parameter \(\lambda\) \[ f(x\mid \lambda) =\lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \,\, 0 < x < \infty. \] Our prior distribution of \(\lambda\) is  the Gamma distribution with parameters \((3,1)\) \[ \pi (\lambda) = \frac{\lambda^2e^{-\lambda}}2, \,\, 0 < x < \infty. \] Let's find posterior distribution \[ \pi(\lambda \mid \mathbf x) \propto \pi(\lambda)  \cdot f(\mathbf x\mid \lambda)= \frac{\lambda^2e^{-\lambda}}2\cdot \lambda e^{-\lambda x_1}\cdot \dots \lambda e^{-\lambda x_{20}}=\lambda^{22}\cdot e^{-\lambda (1+x_1+\dots +x_{20})}\]
It's given that sample mean is \(4.6\) thus \((x_1+\dots +x_{20})/20=4.6\). Hence
\[ \pi(\lambda \mid \mathbf x) \propto \lambda^{22}\cdot e^{-\lambda (1+92)}\] So we have Gamma distribution with parameters \((23,93)\)

Confidence intervals (text)
Assume \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. rv's with distribution \(f(x \mid \theta)\). If \(\theta = \mathsf E X_k\), then the sample mean \(\widehat { \Theta} := \overline{\mathbf X}\) is an unbiased and consistent estimator for \(\theta\). This means \(\mathsf E \widehat{ \Theta} = \theta\) and \(\widehat{ \Theta}\stackrel{\mathsf{P}}{\to} \theta\) as \(n\to\infty\). So most values of \(\widehat{\Theta}\) will be close to \(\theta\) but need not be equal to \(\theta\). For instance if we take sample of odd size \(n=2k+1\) from population with Bernoulli distribution \(X_k \sim \mathscr{B}(1,\theta)\) , we can never get \(\widehat{\theta} = \tfrac12\).
Hence, rather than trying to find estimate, it more useful to find an interval for which we have a certain degree  of confidence that \(\theta\) lies within.
Example.
Assume \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. rv's with normal distribution \(\mathscr{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\). Then the sample mean \( \overline{\mathbf X}\) is an unbiased and consistent estimator for \(\mu\).
As \( \overline{\mathbf X}\sim \mathscr{N}(\mu,\sigma^2/n)\), then \(\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}( \overline{\mathbf X} - \mu) \sim \mathscr{N}(0,1)\). Thus we get \[ \mathsf P\{| \overline{\mathbf X} - \mu| \ge \varepsilon\} = \mathsf P\{ \tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}| \overline{\mathbf X} - \mu| \ge \tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\varepsilon\} =\Phi(-\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\varepsilon) +1-\Phi(\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\varepsilon)=2 \Phi(-\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\varepsilon) \to 0, \, as \, n\to\infty.\] Here \( \Phi\) is c.d.f of standard normal distribution \(Z\sim \mathscr{N}(0,1)\) and since \(Z\) is symetrically distributed, i.e., the p.d.f is an even function, \(f(-x)=f(x)\), we have \[\Phi(-a) = \mathsf P(Z \le - a) = \mathsf P(Z \ge a) = 1 - \mathsf P(Z \le a)\\ = 1 - \Phi(a)\]
Thus for \(n\) large enough, \(\mu\) will be within \(\varepsilon\) of \(\overline{\mathbf X}\) with large probability \(1- 2\Phi(-\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\varepsilon)\): \[ \mathsf P\{|\overline{\mathbf X} - \mu| \le \varepsilon\} = {1- 2 \Phi(-\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\varepsilon)} \to 1 \]
Denote  \(1- 2\Phi(-\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\varepsilon)= 1-\alpha\). Suppose we want to be 95% sure that our mean will be in the interval \( (\overline{\mathbf X} - \varepsilon,\overline{\mathbf X} + \varepsilon)\). It means that we want \(\mathsf P\{|\overline{\mathbf X} - \mu| \le \varepsilon\}=0.95\). Hence \(1- 2 \Phi(-\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\varepsilon)= 1-\alpha=0.95\).
Solving \( 1- \alpha = 1- 2\Phi(-\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\varepsilon), \) we see that \( \Phi(-\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\varepsilon) = \tfrac{\alpha}{2} \)
Therefore, \[ -\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\varepsilon = z_{\alpha/2}. \] Here \(z_{\alpha/2} \) is \(100\alpha/2\)-percentile of normal disribution \( \Phi( z_{\alpha/2}) = \tfrac{\alpha}{2} \) and due to the symmetry of normal distribution \(-z_{\alpha/2}=z_{1-\alpha/2}.\) Hence \[ \varepsilon = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{1-\alpha/2} \]
Therefore, \begin{align*} 1 - \alpha &= \mathsf P\{ |\overline{\mathbf X} - \mu| \le \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}}\} \\ &= \mathsf P\{\overline{\mathbf X} - \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}} \le \mu \le \overline{\mathbf X} + \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}} \} \end{align*} In other words, with probability \(1-\alpha\) the parameter \(\mu\) is inside the interval \[[\overline{\mathbf X} - \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}}, \overline{\mathbf X} + \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}} ]\]
The interval \[[\overline{\mathbf X} - \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}}, \overline{\mathbf X} + \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}} ]\] is called the confidence interval for \(\mu\) of confidence level \(1-\alpha\), or just \(100(1-\alpha)%\) confidence interval  for \(\mu\).
Note that
Increasing confidence level enlarges the length of the interval \(2\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}}\)
Larger \(n\) lead to shorter confidence intervals
Dependence between the length \(2\ell\), confidence \(1-\alpha\), and sample size \(n\): \[ \ell = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}} \]
Definition. Interval estimation.
Let \(a(\mathbf X)\) and \(b(\mathbf X)\) be two statistics satisfying \(a(\mathbf X) \le b(\mathbf X)\) for all \(\mathbf X\). Suppose that on seeing the data \(\mathbf X = \mathbf x\) we make the inference \(a(\mathbf x) \le \theta \le b(\mathbf x)\). Then \([a(\mathbf x), b(\mathbf x)]\) is called an interval estimate and \([a(\mathbf X), b(\mathbf X)]\) is called an interval estimator  of \(\theta\).
Definition. Confidence interval.
Let \(a(\mathbf X)\) and \(b(\mathbf X)\) be two statistics satisfying \(a(\mathbf X) \le b(\mathbf X)\) for all \(\mathbf X\). Assume that \[ \mathsf P\Bigl(a(\mathbf X) \le \theta \le b(\mathbf X)\Bigr) \ge \gamma \] where \(\gamma\) does not depend on \(\theta\).
Then the random interval \([a(\mathbf X), b(\mathbf X)]\) is called a confidence interval for \(\theta\) of confidence level \(\gamma\), or just \(100\gamma%\) confidence interval  for \(\theta\).
In normal family \(\mathscr{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(\mu\) is the location parameter and \(\sigma\) is the scale parameter. More generally,
Definition. Location and scale parameters.
Distribution family \(F_{a,b}\) of rv's \( aX + b \) for a fixed \(X\) has location parameter \(b\in\mathbb R\) and scale parameter \(a>0\).
A general idea for estimation of \(a\) or \(b\) is to get rid of them: \[ Y \sim F_{a,b}, \quad \text{then} \quad (Y-b)/a \sim F_{1,0} \] and the latter is known.
For instance to evaluate \(\mu\) in the example above we use the nomal distribution \(\mathscr{N}(\mu,\sigma^2/n)\) and than get rid of parameters \(\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}( \overline{\mathbf X} - \mu) \sim \mathscr{N}(0,1).\)
Note that \(\mathscr{U}(c,d)\) has location parameter \((c+d)/2\) and the scale parameter \((d-c)/2\). In exponential distribution \(\mathscr{E}(\lambda)\), \(1/\lambda\) is the scale parameter.

Estimation of the mean and variance (text)
Assume \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. rv's with normal distribution \(\mathscr{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\). Then \[\tfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}( \overline{\mathbf X} - \mu) \sim \mathscr{N}(0,1).\] which leads to the interval estimator  \[[\overline{\mathbf X} - \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}}, \overline{\mathbf X} + \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}} ]\]
Confidence interval for \(\mu\), with known \(\sigma\)
Assume \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. rv's with normal distribution \(\mathscr{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\).
The interval \[\Bigl[\overline{\mathbf X} - \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}}, \overline{\mathbf X} + \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}} \Bigl]\] is \(100(1-\alpha)%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\).
What, however, if \(\sigma\) is unknown? We can use estimator of \(\sigma\) instead. For instance, the sample variance \[ S^2 := \frac1{n-1}S_{\mathbf X\mathbf X} = \frac1{n-1}\sum(X_k - \overline{\mathbf X})^2 \] Then \[ T:= \frac{\sqrt{n} (\overline{\mathbf X} - \mu)}{S} = \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}(\overline{\mathbf X} - \mu ) / (S/\sigma) \] has the Student distribution \(\mathscr{T}_{n-1}\) with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom
With \(t^{(n-1)}_\alpha\) denoting the percentile of the Student distribution \(\mathscr{T}_{n-1}\), we find that \[ \mathsf P \Bigl\{ t^{(n-1)}_{\alpha/2} \le \frac{\sqrt{n} (\overline{\mathbf X} - \mu)}{S} \le t^{(n-1)}_{1-\alpha/2} \Bigr\} = 1-\alpha, \] so that \[ \mathsf P \Bigl\{\overline{\mathbf X} - \frac{S}{\sqrt{n}}t^{(n-1)}_{1-\alpha/2} \le \mu \le \overline{\mathbf X} + \frac{S}{\sqrt{n}}t^{(n-1)}_{1-\alpha/2} \Bigr\} = 1-\alpha \]
Confidence interval for \(\mu\), with unknown \(\sigma\)
Assume \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. rv's with normal distribution \(\mathscr{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\).
The interval \[ \Bigl[\overline{\mathbf X} - \frac{S}{\sqrt{n}}t^{(n-1)}_{1-\alpha/2} , \overline{\mathbf X} + \frac{S}{\sqrt{n}}t^{(n-1)}_{1-\alpha/2}\Bigl]\] is called the confidence interval for \(\mu\) of confidence level \(1-\alpha\).
Assume now \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. rv's from some distribution. Let \(\mu = \mathsf E(X_1)\) and \(\sigma^2 = \mathsf{Var}(X_1)\). By the CLT, \(Z:=\sqrt{n}(\overline{\mathbf X} - \mu)/\sigma\) has approximately the standard normal distribution. Therefore,
Approximate confidence interval for \(\mu\), with known \(\sigma\) in case of general distribution.
Assume \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. rv's from some distribution.
The interval \[\Bigl[\overline{\mathbf X} - \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}}, \overline{\mathbf X} + \tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} z_{{1-\alpha/2}} \Bigl]\] is the approximate confidence interval for \(\mu\) of confidence level \(1-\alpha\) .
If \(\sigma\) is unknown, then the approximate confidence interval for the mean is
Approximate confidence interval for \(\mu\), with unknown \(\sigma\) in case of general distribution
Assume \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. rv's from some distribution.
The interval \[ \Bigl[\overline{\mathbf X} - \frac{S}{\sqrt{n}}t^{(n-1)}_{1-\alpha/2} , \overline{\mathbf X} + \frac{S}{\sqrt{n}}t^{(n-1)}_{1-\alpha/2}\Bigl]\] is the approximate confidence interval for \(\mu\) of confidence level \(1-\alpha\).
If \(X_k \sim \mathscr{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \[ S^2 := S_{\mathbf X \mathbf X}/(n-1) \] is an unbiased estimate for \(\sigma^2\).
In particular, \(S_{\mathbf X\mathbf X}/\sigma^2\) has the Pearson \(\chi^2_{n-1}\) distribution.
Therefore, with \(x_{\alpha}^{(n-1)}\) being the percentile of \(\chi^2_{n-1}\), \[ \mathsf P\{ x_{\alpha/2}^{(n-1)} \le (n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \le x_{1-\alpha/2}^{(n-1)}\} = 1-\alpha \]
Confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\) in case normal distribution
Assume \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. rv's with normal distribution \(\mathscr{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\).
The interval \[\Bigl[ \frac{(n-1)S^2}{x_{1-\alpha/2}^{(n-1)}} \frac{(n-1)S^2}{x_{\alpha/2}^{(n-1)}} \Bigl]\] is \(100(1-\alpha)%\) confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\).
Approximate confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\): general distribution
Assume \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. rv's from some distribution.
The interval \[\Bigl[ \frac{(n-1)S^2}{x_{1-\alpha/2}^{(n-1)}} \frac{(n-1)S^2}{x_{\alpha/2}^{(n-1)}} \Bigl]\] is the approximate confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\) of confidence level \(1-\alpha\).
